title: India's Jobs Paradox: Two in Three Unemployed Youth Are Now Graduates
excerpt: Azim Premji University's State of Working India 2026 report reveals that graduate unemployment has remained stuck between 35 and 40 percent for four decades, even as India produces five million graduates a year.
body:
• Nearly 40% of Indian graduates aged 15–25 are unemployed, and graduate unemployment has stayed at 35–40% for four decades straight
  • Two-thirds of all unemployed youth aged 20–29 now hold degrees, up from 46% in 2017, according to the State of Working India 2026 report
  • Of 5 million graduates entering the workforce annually, only 2.8 million find employment — and just 1.7 million land salaried jobs
  • Recent exam-leak protests forced Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation, prompting PM Modi to appoint a Nandan Nilekani–led task force on reforms

India produces more graduates each year than at any point in its history. It also has more educated unemployed people than ever before. According to Azim Premji University's State of Working India 2026 report, two-thirds of unemployed youth between 20 and 29 now hold degrees — up sharply from 46% just six years ago.

The report, which draws on four decades of labour data, puts the graduate unemployment rate at nearly 40% for those aged 15 to 25 and 20% for the 25-to-29 cohort. In absolute terms, 11 million graduates out of 63 million in the 20–29 age group are without work.

A Four-Decade Flatline

The most striking finding in the report is not the scale of the problem but its persistence. Graduate unemployment among young Indians has remained locked between 35 and 40% for forty consecutive years — through economic liberalisation in 1991, the IT boom of the 2000s, and a decade of Make in India and production-linked incentive schemes.

https://x.com/IndiaToday/status/2081739141155598735

Each year, roughly five million graduates enter the Indian labour market. About 2.8 million find some form of employment. Of those, only around 1.7 million secure salaried work — the kind of stable employment that justifies the family investment behind a degree. The remaining 2.2 million join a growing pool of educated, underemployed young people cycling through gig platforms, informal work, and prolonged job searches.

"Only about 51.25% of the youth are deemed employable. In other words, one in two young people are not yet ready for the workforce straight out of college."

— V. Anantha Nageswaran, Chief Economic Adviser, Government of India

Education Expanded, Jobs Did Not

India's higher education infrastructure has grown at a staggering pace. The number of institutions surged from 1,644 at the time of liberalisation to over 69,500 by 2023, with more than 80% now privately operated. Among young women aged 15 to 19, the share staying in education rose from 38% in 1983 to 68% in 2023 — a quiet transformation driven by millions of first-generation aspirant families.

But the labour market failed to keep pace. The share of male graduates aged 20 to 29 working unpaid in family enterprises rose six percentage points to 21% in the five years to 2023, according to the report. Just 54% of male graduates in that age group held salaried jobs — below levels recorded four decades ago.

Among unemployed young graduates tracked for a full year, only 7% obtained permanent salaried employment, the report found. The rest remained in informal work or continued searching.

Protests Force Political Reckoning

The disconnect between degrees and jobs erupted into public view in recent weeks. Thousands of young Indians gathered in New Delhi to protest leaks of medical entrance exam questions — a problem that has plagued competitive exams for years but ignited broader anger over limited opportunities. A Supreme Court judge's comparison of some unemployed youth to cockroaches, later described as misconstrued, added fuel.

Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan stepped down on July 25, and Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced on July 26 a task force on examination reforms led by Infosys co-founder and chair Nandan Nilekani, according to Reuters. Nilekani, the architect of India's Aadhaar digital identity system, is widely respected, but this is India's second committee on exam reforms in as many years.

A Skills Mismatch at Scale

The paradox runs deeper than exam fraud. India's IT services giants — Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, and Wipro — have cut hiring or frozen recruitment even as they report vacancies they cannot fill. TCS has flagged an inability to fill 80,000 positions due to a lack of qualified candidates. Nasscom, the industry body, estimates the sector faces a shortfall of 600,000 skilled professionals.

Less than 5% of India's youth receive formal vocational training, according to the India Employment Report. The Industrial Training Institutes that were designed to bridge the school-to-work gap have expanded threefold since 2005, but quality metrics — pass rates, instructor ratios, and employer linkages — have deteriorated as the system grew.

What Comes Next

India is approaching the peak of its demographic dividend. The share of the working-age population is expected to begin declining after 2030, leaving a narrowing window to convert its young population into an economic asset. With 7.7% GDP growth, the economy is expanding — but not in ways that absorb its graduates.

For many diaspora families who fund educational investments for relatives in India, the data raises difficult questions about returns on those investments. The Nilekani task force will need to move beyond exam security into curriculum reform, industry partnerships, and apprenticeship pathways. Whether New Delhi can translate committee recommendations into structural change will determine if India's demographic window closes as an opportunity seized or a promise broken.
